solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Job notices stirred up protests

indicators.note: something stirred up has been mixed around, so the letters are jumbled into a new order

blocks.note: the two words supply the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: Workers angered by job adverts or dismissal notices take to the streets.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Job notices' reads like the cause of the protests, but its ten letters are simply the raw material.
explanation.definitionFit: Protests and objections are both expressions of disapproval or complaint, so the plural nouns are synonyms.

clue.text: Dotty kind of writing Liberal composed

indicators.note: to compose is to put together or arrange, so the letters are set out afresh

blocks.note: the word supplies the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A slightly mad politician from the Liberal party sits down to write something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dotty' pretends to mean eccentric, but here it literally means made of dots; 'composed' also suggests writing, yet it signals rearranging.
explanation.definitionFit: The tactile script read by blind people consists of patterns of raised dots, hence a dotty kind of writing.

clue.text: Parrot found in Czechoslovakia

indicators.note: something found in a longer word sits inside it, so the letters run unbroken within

blocks.note: letters two to five of the country's name

explanation.surface: A tropical bird turns up in a central European country.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Parrot' looks like the bird, but it is the verb meaning to repeat mindlessly.
explanation.definitionFit: To parrot someone is to repeat their words back without thought, which is what an echo does.

clue.text: Might this underwhelming film get roasted?

definitions.text: Might this underwhelming film get roasted?

blocks.note: surface reading: a poor movie being savaged by the critics
setter's reading: the word for a flop is also a bird cooked in the oven at Christmas

explanation.walkthrough: Critics 'roast' a bad film; the word for a cinematic flop is also the bird that is literally roasted.
explanation.definitionFit: A failed, dreadful film is slang called by the name of a festive roasting bird, and such flops are mocked by reviewers.

clue.text: Bit of cricket? Time the Ashes holder is upset

blocks.note: a set of six balls bowled from one end
T is the abbreviation for time
the Ashes trophy, contested by England and Australia at cricket, is a tiny urn

explanation.surface: A cricket fan grumbles that it is time the side holding the Ashes was beaten.
explanation.walkthrough: An over is six balls in cricket; the Ashes is the England-Australia series whose trophy is a small urn. 'Upset' is a verb here.
explanation.definitionFit: To overturn something is to knock it over or reverse it, which is what upsetting a table or result means.

clue.text: It’s as funny for group of oppressive buggers

indicators.note: funny means odd or peculiar, so the letters end up in a strange arrangement

blocks.note: the two words supply the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: Someone shrugs that a phrase is just as amusing when said about some nasty, rude people.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Buggers' is not an insult here: it means people who plant listening bugs, as East Germany's secret police did.
explanation.definitionFit: The East German secret police oppressed citizens through mass surveillance, including covert microphones in homes.

clue.text: In France I finally meet people like me and globe-trotters

indicators.note: finally points to the end of a word, so only its closing letter is kept

blocks.note: the French word for I
the closing letter of the word
the person writing the clue is a crossword setter

explanation.surface: A traveller in France tells of meeting kindred spirits and other world travellers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'People like me' is the setter speaking about themselves, a common crossword device for SETTER or SETTERS.
explanation.definitionFit: Jet-setters are wealthy people who fly around the world, so they are globe-trotters by habit.

clue.text: Worker who should be very class-conscious?

definitions.text: Worker who should be very class-conscious?

blocks.note: surface reading: someone acutely aware of social rank

blocks.clueFragment: Worker who should be very class-conscious
blocks.note: setter's reading: someone whose job demands attention to a school class of pupils

explanation.walkthrough: Class-conscious normally means preoccupied with social status; here the class is a room of pupils.
explanation.definitionFit: A schoolteacher's working day revolves around the classes of pupils they instruct, so they must be mindful of them.

clue.text: I’m getting tangled with a leotard fitting perfectly

indicators.note: things that get tangled are twisted out of order, so the letters are mixed up

blocks.note: taken as written, apostrophe dropped
taken as written

explanation.surface: A gymnast complains of getting caught up in a leotard that fits a little too snugly.
explanation.walkthrough: The leotard suggests clothing, which makes the tailoring answer hide in plain sight among letters that only need rearranging.
explanation.definitionFit: Clothes made by a tailor to measure suit the wearer exactly, so the term means ideally suited or fitting perfectly.

clue.text: Tips for eggs, venison and darned excellent duck

indicators.note: the tip of something is its very front end, so each word gives its opening letter

blocks.note: the opening letter of each of the five words

explanation.surface: Cooking advice for preparing eggs and venison, plus an exclamation of delight about the duck.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Duck' sits at the end looking like one more food on the menu, but it is the verb and the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To duck a question or a blow is to dodge it, so the verb is a synonym for avoiding something.

clue.text: Python on TV reluctant to make an effort

blocks.note: first meaning: Eric, a member of the Monty Python comedy team
second meaning: lazy

explanation.surface: A snake on television seems too sluggish to do anything.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Python' is not the snake but one of the Monty Python's Flying Circus comedians, Eric of that surname.
explanation.definitionFit: Eric is a famous member of the television comedy troupe, and the adjective also describes someone lazy who avoids work.

clue.text: Are these people in front of supervised gateways?

definitions.text: Are these people in front of supervised gateways?

indicators.note: being in front of something means coming before it, so this piece leads the next

blocks.note: the opening letter of the word
entries are ways in

explanation.surface: Someone wonders whether guards are the people posted outside watched gates.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue describes guards at gates, and also tells you to put the initial of 'supervised' in front of a word for gateways; no first-letter signal is given, which is loose.
explanation.definitionFit: Soldiers on guard duty stand at gates and doorways keeping watch, which is exactly what the whole clue pictures.

clue.text: Eg Mo Salah on the ball, warning of danger

blocks.note: Salah played for Liverpool, whose players are nicknamed the Reds
an idiom for quick-witted and attentive

explanation.surface: A star footballer in possession signals that the opposing defence is in trouble.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On the ball' tempts a footballing reading, but it is the idiom for attentive. Liverpool FC players are called the Reds.
explanation.definitionFit: The highest state of emergency readiness is signalled by this phrase, used for any urgent warning of danger.

clue.text: Means of getting into a tin of good batter

definitions.text: Means of getting into a tin

blocks.clueFragment: Means of getting into a tin
blocks.note: first meaning: a tool for prising open cans
second meaning: a cricketer who starts the innings

explanation.surface: A cook wonders how to get into a tin of ready-made pancake batter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Batter' looks like the kitchen mixture, but it is a cricketer; the best batsmen often open the innings.
explanation.definitionFit: A can tool is called by this name, and so is the cricketer who bats first, usually a reliable one.

clue.text: Messing about, Sartre’s put in detention

indicators.note: messing about means fooling around carelessly, so the letters are thrown into disorder

blocks.note: the philosopher's name supplies the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: The French philosopher, misbehaving as a schoolboy, is kept back after class.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Detention' suggests school punishment, but it means being held in custody.
explanation.definitionFit: Being arrested means being taken into custody by police, a form of detention.

clue.text: Schoolboy’s brief message over newspaper article

indicators.note: in a down clue, over means turned upside down, so the letters run backwards

blocks.note: a short written message
the i is a British national daily paper
the indefinite article

explanation.surface: A pupil writes a short note about an article in the paper.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'i' is a British newspaper, a common crossword source for I. Eton is Britain's best-known boys' boarding school.
explanation.definitionFit: A pupil at Eton College is called by this name, so it is a specific kind of schoolboy.

clue.text: Sadly, capitals of Kansas and Alabama in a state

indicators.note: capitals are the leading letters of words, so only the first of each is kept

blocks.note: an exclamation of regret
the opening letter of each place name

explanation.surface: A lament that the state capitals of two US states are in a mess.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Capitals' suggests state capital cities like Topeka and Montgomery, but means capital letters. 'In a state' also hints at distress.
explanation.definitionFit: The largest of the fifty United States, in the far north-west, is one of the American states.

clue.text: Football club supporter using their hands

blocks.note: Man U, short for Manchester United
an ally supports you

explanation.surface: A football fan who applauds with their hands.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Supporter' points at football fans, but here it means an ally.
explanation.definitionFit: Manual comes from the Latin for hand, so doing something by hand is doing it manually.

clue.text: Tend to hurry up, sure to lose heart

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means read from bottom to top, so the letters run backwards
the heart of a word is its middle, so losing it means the central letters go

blocks.note: to run is to hurry
the word with its middle two letters removed

explanation.surface: Advice that you tend to rush things, and are bound to become discouraged.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tend to' reads as 'be inclined to', but 'Tend' alone is the definition, meaning care for.
explanation.definitionFit: To nurse a patient is to look after them, which is exactly what tending someone means.

clue.text: Illegal drug fine to bring into church

indicators.note: bringing something into a building places it within, so one piece goes inside the other

blocks.note: CE is the Church of England
OK means fine or acceptable

explanation.surface: A shocked remark that someone thinks it acceptable to carry narcotics into a place of worship.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fine' looks like a penalty for smuggling drugs, but it means OK.
explanation.definitionFit: Coke is the common slang name for cocaine, a banned narcotic.

clue.text: Group under pressure in secret scheme

indicators.note: in a down entry, being underneath means coming lower in the column, so this piece follows the other

blocks.note: P is the symbol for pressure in physics
a lot is a group or batch

explanation.surface: A band of conspirators feels the strain while hatching a covert plan.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue, 'under' puts the group below the pressure, so it comes second.
explanation.definitionFit: A plot is a conspiracy planned in private, so it is a covert plan by definition.

clue.text: Awful, covering intro to Genesis’s sad song

indicators.note: an intro is the start of something, so only the opening letter is kept
to cover something is to wrap round it, so one piece sits around the other

blocks.note: dire means dreadful
the opening letter

explanation.surface: A critic pans a rock band's mournful ballad, or perhaps a band covering it.
explanation.walkthrough: Genesis is a rock band, and 'covering' tempts a reading about cover versions of a song.
explanation.definitionFit: A dirge is a slow mournful piece, originally a lament sung at funerals.

clue.text: I feel drunk aboard ship, getting shots

indicators.note: a drunk person staggers about, so the letters reel into a new order
to be aboard a vessel is to be inside it, so one piece goes within the other

blocks.note: the words supply the letters to rearrange
SS is the abbreviation for steamship

explanation.surface: A tipsy passenger on a cruise ship downing glasses of spirits.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shots' suggests drinks to go with 'drunk', but here they are photographs.
explanation.definitionFit: Selfies are photographs people take of themselves, and photographs are commonly called shots.

clue.text: Removing section of complex tract in German

indicators.note: a section is one part of a larger thing, so only a run of letters from the word is used

blocks.note: the final two letters of the word
taken as written
G is the abbreviation for German

explanation.surface: A surgeon cutting out part of a complicated passage in a German patient.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Complex' tempts as an anagram signal for 'tract in', but it gives only its own last two letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Extracting means pulling something out, as a dentist does a tooth, so it is a synonym for removing.
